newsitem.title: FRANCE: French minister says no clash with US over Zaire.
newsitem.headline: French minister says no clash with US over Zaire.

text.p: Foreign Minister Herve de Charette sought on Monday to quash reports of Franco-American differences over the Zaire refugee crisis, saying it saw no conflict of interest over Africa.
"Undoubtedly, in the past weeks, there were some bitter words exchanged between our two countries and I believe such exchanges were unfortunate," de Charette told the daily Le Parisien newspaper.
"But there is no...conflict of interest between France and the United States in Africa.
"France and American are friends and partners although we sometimes analyse things differently," he said.

The French minister was referring both to the Zaire crisis and to a public scrap last month between the U.S. State Department and Jacques Godfrain, France's junior minister for cooperation whose brief is ties with Africa.

Washington angrily complained after Godrain said the U.S. was only interested in Africa at election time and that a visit to the continent by Secretary of State Warren Christopher was aimed at promoting President Bill Clinton's re-election.

Some French newspapers have hinted heavily in past days that apparent U.S. reluctance in joining a peace force to aid refugees caught up in fighting in east Zaire was really aimed at undercutting France's position in Africa.
France, leading a so-far unsuccessful campaign to create such an international force, has been accused by Rwanda and others of favouring the Hutus over the Tutsis in the Zaire crisis.
Critics say Paris is still smarting over loss of influence in neighbouring Rwanda when a Paris-backed, Hutu-led government was overthrown by Tutsi rebels in 1994.
"France has no secret agenda and its goal in this affair (aiding the refugees) is totally altruistic," de Charette told Le Parisien.
"We have no intention of interfering in relations between the countries of the region," de Charette said.

Some, mainly leftist, opponents of French African policy in Paris have accused the government of wanting to send an international force because its very presence would prop up Zaire President Mobutu Sese Seko, also a Paris ally.
The U.S. denied on Monday it was blocking creation of an international force but said it had seen no coherent plan.
De Charette said France was ready to contribute a force of 1,000 to a 5,000-strong which should include U.S., African and European troops.
Paris would like the U.S. to lead the force to give it more influence and to avert accusations that it was a French-led effort to press colonial interests.
De Charette told Le Parisien that Italy, Spain, the Netherlands and several French former African colonies had indicated readiness to join.

De Charette, who accused the world last week of "spinelessness" in its reaction to the events in Zaire, said the world would witness "one of the greatest dramas in the history of humanity" if it failed to intervene.

Bernard Debre, Godfrain's predecessor as cooperation minister, wrote in the daily newspaper Le Figaro that a solution to the crisis could be the creation a separate Hutu state with territory taken from Zaire, Rwanda and Burundi.

Although a member of the ruling RPR Gaullist party and brother to serving Interior Minister Jean-Louis Debre, Bernard Debre is on cool terms with President Jacques Chirac and not believed to wield influence on French African policy.
